masthead.footnote: *Anybody can start a podcast without spending anything except their time. Page 2

brief.head: Speed it up
brief.text: Our brains can take in 500 words a minute, Amit Varma said. Raise lis­ten­ing speed in steps until one stops feel­ing nor­mal: that is your level. {049-C02}

brief.head: Cursed by knowing
brief.text: Know a sub­ject too well and you as­sume lis­ten­ers share your base­line, Varma warned. In audio they can­not go back, so set scenes and in­tro­duce voices quickly. {049-C10}

brief.head: Patience pays
brief.text: Work for love and you keep im­prov­ing; chase the num­bers and you lose your soul. Creators over­es­ti­mate the short term and un­der­es­ti­mate the long[[x6]], Varma said. {049-C19}

brief.head: Loved by a few
brief.text: Many chan­nels can av­er­age about fif­teen sec­onds of view­ing; Varma’s lis­ten­ing ses­sions av­er­age about forty min­utes[[x8]]. Better to be loved by a few than liked by many[[x7]], he said. {049-C20}

brief.head: Do it in Hindi
brief.text: English pod­casts in India are sat­u­rated, Varma said. If your English is a hun­dred and your Hindi eighty, do Hindi[[x9]]: that au­di­ence needs you more. {049-C21}

thought.label: Thought for the day
thought.text: Perfection is the enemy of pro­duc­tion.

lead.kicker: Amit Varma gives away his podcasting course
lead.head: The long and short of podcasting

pic.caption: Ajay Shah (left) and Amit Varma early in Episode 49

body: Amit Varma used to teach a three-week course on pod­cast­ing. He has de­cided never to teach it again. In this episode he gave the whole thing away, promis­ing to talk “as long as the light lasts”.
Ajay Shah in­tro­duced him as the man who pi­o­neered the pod­cast in India, be­fore he “be­came a world fa­mous in­ven­tor and pro­ducer of a YouTube show”.

Varma began with a con­fes­sion. When *The Seen and the Unseen* started seven years ago, he planned episodes of 15 or 20 min­utes[[x1]], sure that at­ten­tion spans were short[[x2]]. “I was wrong about ev­ery­thing I thought I knew about pod­cast­ing,” he said.

The episodes grew to three and four hours, then to oral his­to­ries of seven and eight hours. “And as it got longer and longer, I got more and more love from peo­ple.” {049-S01} By his con­ser­va­tive es­ti­mate, lis­ten­ers have spent about 20 mil­lion hours with the show.
## The case for audio

Audio, Varma said, is not YouTube with­out the video. People lis­ten while com­mut­ing, run­ning or wash­ing dishes, so they are a cap­tive au­di­ence. Many lis­ten at higher speeds and lose no nu­ance. And they want depth, which the rest of the media, a mile wide and an inch deep, does not give them.
“Attention spans are not the prob­lem,” he said. {049-C01}
Nor is a pod­cast radio on de­mand. Radio, in his metaphor, speaks to four peo­ple in a car. “Podcasting is a voice in your head.” {049-C04}

That in­ti­macy brings two im­per­a­tives: re­spect lis­ten­ers, who are ac­com­plished peo­ple and often know more than the host, and be your­self. Asked which gap in the mar­ket to fill, Varma replied: “There is only one gap in the mar­ket. You aren’t there.” {049-C05}
## Stories and con­ver­sa­tions
Varma di­vides pod­casts into two kinds: sto­ry­telling and con­ver­sa­tion.

For sto­ry­tellers, his tips came from writ­ing: one piece of in­for­ma­tion at a time, show rather than tell, be­ware the curse of knowl­edge, and make every sen­tence and sound ef­fect take the story for­ward or deeper. One per­son is enough, he said, as Dan Carlin’s *Hardcore History* proves.
For con­ver­sa­tions, the rules are about the guest. Ignore con­ven­tions of length. Define your pur­pose. Do your re­search. Never in­ter­rupt. Follow the flow, not the list of ques­tions.
Shah, ask­ing the ques­tions, added ex­am­ples of his own: Paul Simon on why songs are lin­ear, and a friend who learnt new things from one episode about a man she had known for fif­teen years.
## Get it done

The last lessons were for cre­ators. Have a bias for ac­tion. Play the long game, be­cause or­ganic growth is ex­po­nen­tial and looks like noth­ing for a long time. Be loved by a few rather than liked by many. And think out of the box, in­clud­ing about which lan­guage to pod­cast in.
Varma had slides on equip­ment too, but the light was run­ning out. He squeezed in ad­vice on mi­cro­phones and promised a doc­u­ment of notes in the show notes.
His ver­dict on cost: “The spoiler alert is that you can re­ally do it for very cheap or you can do it for free.” {049-C22}
His last words went back to his first les­son for cre­ators: “Have a bias for ac­tion, don’t hes­i­tate.”

second.label: Turning down a laureate
second.head: Three hours or nothing
second.deck: Amit Varma said no to a Nobel winner in the week of his prize

pic.caption: Amit Varma on turning down a Nobel laureate

body: A pub­lisher rang Amit Varma with an offer: fly to Delhi and record with Abhijit Banerjee[[x3]] in the week he won the Nobel Prize. Varma asked for three hours. The pub­lisher of­fered one. He said no. {049-S08}

One hour, he said, would have meant talk­ing only about what Banerjee won the prize for, RCTs, a nar­row sub­ject. With three, Varma wanted to begin in 1963, when Banerjee’s fa­ther taught his own fa­ther at Presidency College, Calcutta: “a pre­his­tory of the man”.

Given five to eight hours, he could imag­ine never men­tion­ing the work at all. People and their jour­neys in­ter­est him more. And there are, he said, “fifty other peo­ple who will record with you”.

quote.text: I don’t care what kind of celebrity you are.

third.head: Not a word from the host

pic.caption: Amit Varma on Mrinal Pande’s first answer

body: Amit Varma asked Mrinal Pande[[x4]] his first ques­tion. She then spoke for more than an hour, and he did not say a word. {049-S12}
In a mix of Hindi and English, she took lis­ten­ers from her child­hood in the 1950s to the end of the 1970s: her par­ents, her mother, her sis­ters, her com­ing of age as a woman.

“And it would have been a dis­as­ter to in­ter­rupt at any point,” Varma said. A younger, cal­lower ver­sion of him­self might have done it; other in­ter­view­ers would have cut in after two min­utes, and she would never have gone so deep.
Not in­ter­rupt­ing is an ar­ti­cle of faith[[x5]] for him. Most of us, he said, quot­ing Stephen Covey, “lis­ten to re­spond, we don’t lis­ten to un­der­stand.” {049-C14}

box.title: The course he gave away
box.text: Amit Varma taught a three-week pod­cast­ing course twice a year, to a niche au­di­ence. He has now de­cided he will never teach it again. Instead, he said, he wants to give away ev­ery­thing he has learnt. {#course}

sections.label: Why audio
sections.head: Captive, quick and deep
sections.caption: when, how and why we listen
body: When Amit Varma began *The Seen and the Unseen*, he thought lis­ten­ers had to be grabbed in 15 sec­onds and let go within 20 min­utes. Three rea­sons proved him wrong.
The first is when peo­ple lis­ten: com­mut­ing, work­ing out, doing chores. A run­ner is a cap­tive au­di­ence.

The sec­ond is how. “Our brain can com­pre­hend up to five hun­dred words a minute,” Varma said, while we speak at 160 to 200. {#brain} Raise the speed in steps, to 1.2x and then 1.5x, until one step stops feel­ing nor­mal: that is your nat­u­ral level. {049-C02}
## Mush at six times
Varma lis­tens to most things at 2x, and up to 3x for re­search. Krish Ashok once told him of a blind col­league who lis­tens at 6x. “Now you see the plas­tic­ity of the brain,” he said. {049-S02}

The third rea­son is why. Everybody craves depth, Varma ar­gued, and the rest of the media is a mile wide and an inch deep. “Attention spans are not the prob­lem. When you want to go deep, you can go deep. And the most ef­fi­cient way of going deep is audio.” {049-C01}

Ajay Shah, for whom faster lis­ten­ing was “a very new dis­cov­ery”, dis­agreed on depth. “Most hu­mans want di­ver­sion,” he said; only a tiny frac­tion crave depth, and that is enough. Varma replied that ev­ery­one has the ca­pac­ity for it.
~ His first episode with Karthik Muralidharan ran three hours and fif­teen min­utes. Transcribed, it came to 45,000 words, half a reg­u­lar book. {#muralidharan}

quote.text: And one should not be judg­men­tal about what you lis­ten at. What you lis­ten at is what you lis­ten at.

sections.label: Why podcasts
sections.head: Not radio with a pause button
sections.caption: a voice in your head
body: Ajay Shah’s first thought was that pod­cast­ing was time-shifted radio: the 9 pm news his fa­ther once tuned in for, now on de­mand. Amit Varma said it is fun­da­men­tally dif­fer­ent.
In India, he said, li­cence fees for an FM chan­nel are in­cred­i­bly high, so sta­tions chase the low­est com­mon de­nom­i­na­tor to re­coup them. {#fm} FM is not even al­lowed to do news.

A pod­cast costs noth­ing but time and needs no li­cence. So it can find niches no­body sus­pected, such as lis­ten­ers for eight-hour con­ver­sa­tions: a niche that, Varma said, “did not know it ex­isted”. {049-C03}
## Closer and closer

Cinema is a big screen far away, made for west­erns and car chases. Television sits two or three me­tres off and suits sit­coms; YouTube is half a metre away. Radio speaks to four peo­ple in a car. “Podcasting is a voice in your head[[x12]],” Varma said. {049-C04}
So voice mod­u­la­tion would be a bug, not a fea­ture. One lis­tener of his episode with Abhinandan Sekhri[[x13]] felt so at home that he in­ter­rupted the record­ing. {049-S03}

~ Shah had his own ev­i­dence. Anjali Sharma had known Josh Felman for fif­teen years, yet his episode told her things that were new. Felman’s reply: “You never asked me, oth­er­wise I would have al­ways told you.” {049-S04}

quote.text: I felt so much that I’m sit­ting in a liv­ing room talk­ing to two of my friends that at one point I in­ter­rupted you.
quote.who: A listener, as quoted by Amit Varma

sections.label: Two imperatives
sections.head: Respect them, be yourself
sections.caption: respecting listeners and being yourself
body: Old media had the few talk­ing down to the many, Amit Varma said: con­de­scend­ing, pa­tro­n­is­ing, lec­tur­ing. An in­ti­mate medium does not allow it.

Listeners are ac­com­plished peo­ple who in many ways know more than the host. So the first im­per­a­tive is to re­spect their time and speak to them as human be­ings. No ar­ti­fice, he said, is re­quired.

The sec­ond is to be au­then­tic. When a par­tic­i­pant in his pod­cast­ing course asked whether there was a gap in the mar­ket to fill, Varma said it was a ter­ri­ble way to think. Among more than seven bil­lion peo­ple, only one thing sets you apart: that you are you. {049-C05}
## A jour­ney, not a mar­ket

*The Seen and the Unseen*, he said, is his in­tel­lec­tual jour­ney: he calls peo­ple he wants to know more about, not peo­ple in the news. Listeners on a sim­i­lar jour­ney, at what­ever point, will come along.

Asked by Ajay Shah whether he de­signs for loyal fans or oc­ca­sional vis­i­tors, Varma said he does not think of the au­di­ence at all: “Ekla chalo re”, walk alone, “and then who­ever comes comes along”. {049-J15}

~ A loyal au­di­ence that turns up every Friday is al­ready form­ing for *Everything is Everything*, Varma said. Even so, when the two started the show, he asked Shah not to look at the num­bers for two years, about 104 episodes. {049-S16}

quote.text: There is only one gap in the mar­ket. You aren’t there.

sections.label: Storytelling
sections.head: One thing at a time, please
sections.caption: telling stories for the ear
body: A reader can go back over a sen­tence. A lis­tener wash­ing dishes can­not, Amit Varma said, so audio should give one piece of in­for­ma­tion at a time. {049-C06}[[x14]]

His print ex­am­ple had “the fa­mous pod­caster Amit Varma”, while con­duct­ing a we­bi­nar from his home of­fice in Andheri, ar­rested by the Delhi po­lice for pol­lut­ing Delhi with his con­vo­luted classes. The audio ver­sion opened: “The fa­mous pod­caster Amit Varma is be­hind bars.”
Ajay Shah re­called Paul Simon on poems and songs: the mind goes over a poem many times, but “Songs are lin­ear. So you don’t get a sec­ond take.” {049-S06}
## Show, don’t tell

Listeners stay, Varma said, be­cause they care about a char­ac­ter and want to know how a con­flict re­solves. Kurt Vonnegut’s rule: every char­ac­ter must want some­thing, even if it is only a glass of water. {049-C07}

Showing means fewer ad­jec­tives and more verbs, as in the film cliché of the scene where a char­ac­ter pets a dog. “All of the ac­tion of the world, all of the in­ter­est in the world is in verbs.” {049-C08}

~ Every sen­tence, and every sound ef­fect, must take the story for­ward or deeper. *Everything is Everything* learnt this with on-screen in­serts: these days, a men­tion of Karl Marx brings no photo of him. {049-C09}

quote.text: Because what draws us into the story, it is that want­ing, it is that de­sire.

portraits.caption: Kurt Vonnegut
portraits.credit: Bernard Gotfryd / Adam Cuerden, public domain

sections.label: Conversation
sections.head: Out of autocomplete mode
sections.caption: the art of conversation
body: Amit Varma does not in­ter­view peo­ple, he said; he has con­ver­sa­tions. His first rule is to ig­nore con­ven­tions of length, and he cred­its him­self with shift­ing India’s Overton win­dow: two- and three-hour episodes are now nor­mal.

Form dic­tates con­tent. For a five-minute show you need not read the guest’s book; for half an hour, a ChatGPT sum­mary will do; for an hour, you must read it. For eight hours, read ev­ery­thing[[x15]] they have writ­ten, and care about their life. {049-C11}

Authors ar­rive with pre­pared sound bites, able to talk on au­topi­lot. Varma asks about child­hood and home, and lets him­self be vul­ner­a­ble. “And my task is to take them out of au­to­com­plete mode.” {049-C12}
## Follow the thread

Panel mod­er­a­tors, he said, are often think­ing of ques­tion seven while the guest an­swers ques­tion six. He pre­pares themes in depth, in no fixed order. “That path is where the magic lies.” {049-C15}
For his long­est episodes he works with “three over­lap­ping scaf­fold­ings”: the guest’s life, their work, and themes and ideas. {049-C16}

~ Clarity in­cludes tense. Ajay Shah re­called being thrown, in the episode on the 1991 re­forms, by Shruti Rajagopalan nar­rat­ing his­tory in the present tense. His rule: past tense for the past. {049-S13}

quote.text: And then I will find that I haven’t used eighty per cent of the prep that I have done, and it doesn’t mat­ter.

art.caption: Amit Varma on the art of conversation

sections.label: For creators
sections.head: Doers versus whiners
sections.caption: a bias for action
body: Abraham Lincoln, Amit Varma re­called, would spend five of six hours sharp­en­ing the axe[[x16]] be­fore chop­ping down a tree. {049-J14} That suits pol­icy, Varma said, but cre­ators should do the op­po­site. “If you’re faced with a choice of get­ting it right and get­ting it done, I want you to get it done.” {049-C17}
Everyone is bad at first; he tells peo­ple to hear *The Seen and the Unseen* in re­verse order. “You have to cut the tree to learn how to cut the tree.”

Ajay Shah’s motto since child­hood is that life is not a spec­ta­tor sport: play­ing cricket him­self mat­ters more than watch­ing Sachin Tendulkar. He wants a cul­ture that trea­sures people’s best work, so that ev­ery­one is read­ier to start. {049-C18}

At the XKDR Forum an­niver­sary party, asked to com­plete “There are two kinds of peo­ple in the world”, Varma had said: the doers and the whin­ers[[x17]]. {#whiners} “And you have de­scribed the whin­ers,” he told Shah.
## The long game
The YouTuber Ali Abdaal reached his thou­sandth sub­scriber only around his fifti­eth video. His later ad­vice: two videos a week for two years, with­out look­ing at the num­bers. {049-S15}
~ Shah added that an in­au­then­tic show can last only so long be­fore its maker loses in­ter­est.

quote.text: Now most peo­ple are not going to make fifty videos when they have less than a thou­sand sub­scribers.
So the kind of form will dic­tate the kind of con­tent. And the kind of con­tent will dic­tate your char­ac­ter. It will change you. You do a longer pod­cast, you will lis­ten much more.

p3.title: Stories from the studio
p3.deck: A railway driver, an unmentioned book, a clipped guest and a generous one

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on a 1957 landmark of radio, and show, don’t tell
stories.head: The driver who stayed on board
body: John Axon was a rail­way driver. At one point, Amit Varma said, he was driv­ing a train that he knew he could not con­trol: it was going to ca­reen out. {049-S07}
He had two choices. He could jump and save him­self, or stay on the train and do what­ever he could to save lives up ahead. He stayed on the train, and he died.

A group of peo­ple wrote a bunch of songs about him. They also went to his vil­lage and recorded in­ter­views with the peo­ple who had known him, with no plan to use any of it. They took the sound of the train, the back­ground, the fam­ily, some­one cry­ing.

“And then they had the mas­ter stroke that why don’t we use all of this?” Varma said. “And they used it.” The re­sult was *The Ballad of John Axon*, from 1957, which Varma was un­sure whether to call a play or an album. {049-R03}
Hearing some­body who knew Axon talk about him, Varma said, tells you far more than being told that his vil­lagers con­sid­ered him a good guy.

He paired it with a sec­ond land­mark, *Sun of the Family*, a Danish radio show from around 1997 about a young mu­si­cian who killed him­self. Its pro­duc­ers spoke to his par­ents, his brother and his girl­friend. {049-R04}
~ “It is heart­break­ing when you lis­ten to it,” Varma said. In the in­flec­tion of their voices and in their par­tic­u­lar mem­o­ries, a whole per­son comes to life.
stories.why: This is show, don’t tell in sound. Hearing the peo­ple who knew a man talk about him does more than any narrator’s ad­jec­tive, and Varma’s rule for all sto­ry­telling is fewer ad­jec­tives, more verbs. {049-C08}
stories.postscript: Varma did not know whether *Sun of the Family* is on­line, and asked lis­ten­ers to put it in the com­ments if it is.

pic.caption: Amit Varma on the ballad of a railway driver

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on preparing hard, then letting it go
stories.head: Notes for a book never mentioned
body: On a trip to Bangalore, record­ing some six episodes in seven days, Amit Varma was due to record one morn­ing with Sugata Srinivasaraju, who had just pub­lished a mas­sive book on Deve Gowda, *Furrows in a Field*. {049-R13}
He stayed up all night and wrote sev­eral thou­sand words of notes on it. “The next day we met, we spoke for five and a half hours, we did not men­tion the book.” {049-S09}

Srinivasaraju’s life, the mi­lieu he grew up in and how he watched his city trans­form were so fas­ci­nat­ing that the book was never needed. And Varma is his own boss: no radio sta­tion was telling him to spend 45 min­utes on the book.
~ Search YouTube for Sugata on Deve Gowda, he said, and you find fifty talks and forty panel dis­cus­sions, but not what they spoke about for five hours.
stories.why: Preparation is not for show­ing off. Varma says he often finds he has not used 80 per cent of his prep, and it does not mat­ter: it is what lets him fol­low a bet­ter con­ver­sa­tion. {049-C13}

pic.caption: Amit Varma on an all-night preparation

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on a guest he admires, and a flow that never came
stories.head: Ask, answer, stop, repeat
body: Amit Varma ad­mires Tyler Cowen, whose in­ter­view­ing style is, in a sense, the polar op­po­site of his own. {#cowen} Cowen brings a set of great pre­pared ques­tions, “the kind of ques­tions that some­one like me is not even ca­pa­ble of com­ing up with”, and goes through them one after an­other.
Then Cowen came on *The Seen and the Unseen*, in a re­mote record­ing. Varma asked a ques­tion; Cowen an­swered it and stopped. Another ques­tion, an­other clipped an­swer. {049-S10}
Varma never found the flow he looks for. “It’s not his fault, it’s not my fault, we are who we are,” he said.
~ If he recorded five hours with Cowen today, he said, he would treat it very dif­fer­ently. There is no right or wrong way to do it.

quote.text: So it’s a weird kind of like two op­po­site styles col­lid­ing.

stories.postscript: Varma once com­plained that Ajay Shah’s an­swers were too short as well. Shah, he says, has loos­ened up a lot since.

pic.caption: Amit Varma on two opposite styles colliding

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on guests who send listeners to other guests
stories.head: Have you heard the other one?
body: In mid-April, a cou­ple of days be­fore this episode was recorded, Jerry Pinto and Shanta Gokhale were sign­ing books in ad­join­ing queues at a book event. A reader told Pinto that his episode of *The Seen and the Unseen* had been trans­for­ma­tional. {049-S11}
Pinto’s reply, as it was re­lated to Amit Varma: “That is okay, but have you heard his episode with Shanta ji?”

Gokhale’s episode ran eight and a half hours. She is 83, and when some­one asked why so long, Varma an­swered: “One hour for each decade of her life. Are you telling me that is suf­fi­cient?” {049-J05}
~ Pinto’s own episode ran eight hours[[x18]]. In it, Varma and Pinto teared up to­gether while talk­ing about their moth­ers. {049-R17}
stories.why: One guest send­ing a fan to an­other is val­i­da­tion of a rare kind. It also shows Varma’s method at work: when the host is vul­ner­a­ble, guests drop their pre­pared sound bites and open up in re­turn. {049-C12}

quiz.q: Which three things, according to Amit Varma, explain why audio listeners will stay for hours?
quiz.a: When they lis­ten, how they lis­ten and why: cap­tive, at higher speeds, want­ing depth.

quiz.q: How fast does Krish Ashok’s blind colleague listen to audio, and what does it show?
quiz.a: At 6x, which shows how far the brain’s plas­tic­ity lets it ad­just.

quiz.q: In Varma’s distance metaphor, if radio is four people in a car, what is a podcast?
quiz.a: A voice in your head, which he calls the most in­ti­mate medium.

quiz.q: Why did Varma turn down an episode with an economist in his Nobel Prize week?
quiz.a: The pub­lisher of­fered one hour; he wanted three, to start in 1963.

quiz.q: What kept confusing Ajay Shah in the episode on the 1991 reforms with Shruti Rajagopalan?
quiz.a: She nar­rated past events in the present tense, a mod­ern American habit, he said.

quiz.q: If your English is a hundred and your Hindi eighty, what does Varma advise?
quiz.a: Do Hindi: English pod­casts are sat­u­rated, and that au­di­ence needs you more.

Beneath one’s dig­nity; Varma says pod­cast­ing in Hindi is not.

p4.credits: Everything is Everything was Amit Varma and Ajay Shah’s weekly show, 128 episodes from June 2023 to December 2025. This edition is made from Episode 49. The moving pictures, stills and chapter cards are from its video; the chapter art is by Simahina. Every play button starts the video at the moment it was said. The articles and headlines were written by Claude, an AI model, from the episode’s machine-made transcript, and checked against it. Other photographs are from Wikimedia Commons: Tyler Cowen (Tyler Cowen, CC BY-SA 3.0); Paul Simon (Matthew Straubmuller (imatty35), CC BY 2.0); Kurt Vonnegut (Bernard Gotfryd / Adam Cuerden, public domain); Kevin Kelly (Cmichel67, CC BY-SA 4.0); Russell Roberts (Russell Roberts, CC BY-SA 4.0). The covers on the shelf are from Amazon and Apple.

shelf.title: Hardcore History
shelf.creator: Dan Carlin
shelf.why: One man reads around forty books per episode and then sim­ply talks, with no script, co-host or sound ef­fects, and it is riv­et­ing.

shelf.title: Blueprint for Armageddon
shelf.creator: Dan Carlin
shelf.why: The Hardcore History se­ries that kept Amit out­side his build­ing after runs, weep­ing in the rain: the let­ters sol­diers wrote to their wives and girl­friends the night be­fore a reck­less mis­sion in which they all died taught him the power of audio sto­ry­telling, along with lessons on re­silience, tragedy and the folly of na­tion states.

shelf.title: The Ballad of John Axon
shelf.why: A land­mark in audio his­tory.

shelf.title: Sun of the Family
shelf.why: The pro­duc­ers in­ter­viewed his par­ents, brother and girl­friend, and a whole per­son comes alive through the in­flec­tions in their voices and their par­tic­u­lar mem­o­ries.

shelf.title: EconTalk
shelf.creator: Russ Roberts
shelf.why: Russ Roberts’s pod­cast, a long-time favourite of Amit’s and the clos­est to his own ap­proach: re­laxed, con­ver­sa­tional and deep, fo­cused on ideas rather than the guest’s life.

shelf.title: Conversations with Tyler
shelf.creator: Tyler Cowen
shelf.why: Cowen asks great pre­pared ques­tions, which Amit says some­one like him couldn’t even come up with, and moves through them crisply.

shelf.title: A Meditation on Form
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Amit’s essay on how form dic­tates con­tent: long-form pod­cast­ing is a dif­fer­ent ac­tiv­ity from short-form, not a longer ver­sion of it, and its pa­tience, lis­ten­ing and cu­rios­ity changed him as a host and per­haps as a per­son.

shelf.title: 1000 True Fans
shelf.creator: Kevin Kelly
shelf.why: Kevin Kelly’s ar­gu­ment that cre­ators don’t need scale: a thou­sand true fans pay­ing $100 a year is a liv­ing, wher­ever in the world they are.

shelf.title: 100 True Fans
shelf.creator: Li Jin
shelf.why: Li Jin’s more con­cen­trated ver­sion of Kevin Kelly’s idea: a hun­dred fans pay­ing $1,000 a year give a cre­ator the same in­come from a smaller, more com­mit­ted au­di­ence.

shelf.title: Sinocism
shelf.creator: Bill Bishop
shelf.why: Bishop isn’t a main­stream name, and he writes about China in a way so spe­cialised that main­stream out­lets might never com­mis­sion him.

shelf.title: How I Gained 1 MILLION Subscribers
shelf.creator: Ali Abdaal
shelf.why: Ali Abdaal’s growth graph shows ex­po­nen­tial growth in prac­tice: al­most noth­ing for a long time (about 1,000 sub­scribers after 50 videos and half a year), then a near-vertical line.

shelf.title: My Top 10 Tips for Aspiring YouTubers
shelf.creator: Ali Abdaal
shelf.why: Advice Amit takes se­ri­ously be­cause it comes from some­one who has done it: make two videos a week for two years and don’t look at the num­bers, the an­ti­dote to quit­ting while you’re still bad.

shelf.title: Furrows in a Field
shelf.creator: Sugata Srinivasaraju
shelf.why: Amit calls it a great book, even though their five-and-a-half-hour con­ver­sa­tion never got to it.

shelf.title: The Rooted Cosmopolitanism of Sugata Srinivasaraju (Episode 277, The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma & Sugata Srinivasaraju
shelf.why: Five and a half hours on Sugata Srinivasaraju’s life, the mi­lieu he grew up in and how he watched his city trans­form, of­fer­ing an ideal Amit calls ‘a treasure’: being both rooted and cos­mopoli­tan.

shelf.title: Playwright at the Centre
shelf.creator: Shanta Gokhale
shelf.why: Amit calls it a great book on the his­tory of Marathi the­atre.

shelf.title: The Life and Times of Shanta Gokhale (Episode 311, The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma & Shanta Gokhale
shelf.why: An eighty-three-year-old woman of many parts, given roughly one hour per decade of her life.

shelf.title: The Life and Times of Jerry Pinto (Episode 314, The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma & Jerry Pinto
shelf.why: An eight-and-a-half-hour oral his­tory that Amit calls per­haps his most mem­o­rable, and the episode through which many lis­ten­ers find the show.

shelf.title: The Life and Times of Mrinal Pande (Episode 263, The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma & Mrinal Pande
shelf.why: A first-hand por­trait of a leg­endary Hindi writer who wrote within the con­straints of run­ning a house­hold.

shelf.title: Natasha Badhwar Lives the Examined Life (Episode 301, The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma & Natasha Badhwar
shelf.why: Natasha Badhwar, who home­schools her chil­dren, on par­ent­ing, writ­ing and how to ed­u­cate your kids; Amit calls it his ‘per­fect episode’ for its bal­ance and a gen­er­ous guest.

shelf.title: The Life and Times of Nilanjana Roy (Episode 284, The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma & Nilanjana Roy
shelf.why: Over 5 hours 45 min­utes it leaned heav­ily on ideas and never reached her years in jour­nal­ism.

shelf.title: The Life and Times of KP Krishnan (Episode 355, The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma & KP Krishnan
shelf.why: An eight-hour oral his­tory from a re­former in­side the Indian state: how India han­dled the 2008 cri­sis, fought for in­fla­tion tar­get­ing and built the bank­ruptcy code.

shelf.title: Josh Felman Tries to Make Sense of the World (Episode 321, The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma & Josh Felman
shelf.why: A con­ver­sa­tion with Josh Felman, whom Amit calls a great thinker, that re­vealed things about him even Ajay, a friend of fif­teen years, had never heard.

shelf.title: Episode of The Seen and the Unseen with Ramachandra Guha
shelf.creator: Amit Varma & Ramachandra Guha
shelf.why: Amit’s first two episodes with Ramachandra Guha, on Gandhi, for which Amit read some thirty books, so they dis­til a whole shelf of bi­ogra­phies.

shelf.title: The Life and Times of Abhinandan Sekhri (Episode 254, The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma & Abhinandan Sekhri
shelf.why: The lis­tener felt he was sit­ting in a liv­ing room with two friends, so much so that he in­ter­rupted them.

shelf.title: Fixing Indian Education (Episode 185, The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma & Karthik Muralidharan
shelf.why: A deep dive with Karthik Muralidharan into what’s bro­ken in Indian ed­u­ca­tion and how to fix it, in­clud­ing his point that the sys­tem is op­ti­mised for sort­ing, not teach­ing.

shelf.title: A Scientist in the Kitchen (Episode 204, The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma & Krish Ashok
shelf.why: Krish Ashok on the sci­ence and ori­gins of Indian food, with the story of a blind col­league who lis­tens to audio at 6x speed, Amit’s favourite ex­am­ple of how much the brain can adapt.

shelf.title: The Importance of the 1991 Reforms (Episode 237, The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma, Shruti Rajagopalan & Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Shruti Rajagopalan and Ajay on what 1991 achieved and left un­done (fac­tor mar­kets, agri­cul­ture), and how free­ing parts of the econ­omy set off the dis­cov­ery and trade be­hind India’s growth spurt.

shelf.title: The Greatest Productivity Mantra: Kaator Re Bhaaji! (Episode 11, Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma & Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The show’s pro­duc­tiv­ity mantra: be­tween a great idea and its re­al­i­sa­tion lies drudgery, and the rem­edy is to keep doing the work until magic hap­pens.

shelf.title: 4 Papers That Changed the World (Episode 41, Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma & Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The hosts ex­plain land­mark pa­pers in plain lan­guage, no­tably Coase on why firms exist and Hayek on how prices co­or­di­nate a so­ci­ety no plan­ner can grasp.

shelf.title: Long As I Can See The Light
shelf.creator: Chris Cornell
shelf.why: A mu­si­cal wink that fits an episode lit­er­ally recorded until the day­light ran out.

shelf.title: ATR2100x microphone
shelf.creator: Audio-Technica
shelf.why: It is a dy­namic mic, so it picks up only what is close to it, which suits a home setup bet­ter than a stu­dio con­denser mic.

shelf.title: Anchor
shelf.why: Free host­ing for your first episodes, which you can start record­ing on a mo­bile phone.

shelf.title: Art of Podcasting: Brasstacks (notes PDF)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Covers the tech­ni­cal de­tails of start­ing a pod­cast that he couldn’t get through on cam­era.

shelf.title: The Art of Clear Writing
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Amit’s writ­ing course, which treats clear writ­ing as a test of clear think­ing.

laughs.text: To show what not to do in audio, Amit writes a sen­tence about his own ar­rest: ‘The fa­mous pod­caster Amit Varma, while con­duct­ing a we­bi­nar on writ­ing from his home of­fice in Andheri, Mumbai, was ar­rested by the Delhi po­lice for the crime of mak­ing Delhi more pol­luted by broad­cast­ing his con­vo­luted classes there.’ The se­quel: he ‘protested his in­no­cence be­fore the of­fi­cers in khaki, one of whom he be­rated for using an ad­verb.’ The ver­sion rewrit­ten for audio be­gins: ‘The fa­mous pod­caster Amit Varma is be­hind bars.’

Amit mimes jog­ging while de­scrib­ing a typ­i­cal lis­tener, Ajay smiles, and Amit de­mands, ‘Why did you smile when I did this?’ He drops the jog­ger for some­one wash­ing dishes. When he ges­tures again, the lis­tener ends up ‘wash­ing dishes on an el­e­vated plat­form.’

Amit’s sign-off as the day­light fades: ‘one piece of tech­nol­ogy that you and I can­not con­trol, Ajay Shah, even in these mod­ern times, is the sun... the sun is kind of set­ting on us, but lit­er­ally, not metaphor­i­cally, and not even lit­er­ally be­cause the sun isn’t set­ting, the earth is turn­ing.’

Robert McKee, whom Amit de­scribes as the au­thor of many great books on sto­ry­telling: ‘story is a nat­u­ral form of thought.’ Amit uses it to argue that audio is the old­est form of sto­ry­telling.

Margaret Atwood: ‘A word after a word after a word is power.’ Kurt Vonnegut: ‘every char­ac­ter must want some­thing, even if it is only a glass of water.’ Amit pairs them on why you can never take the listener’s at­ten­tion for granted.
